paragraphs.text: London's coffeehouses were establishments which primarily served prepared coffee or other hot beverages. They differed from restaurants in that only light snacks were available, rather than meals. Coffeehouses largely served as centres where patrons could meet, talk, write, read, entertain one another, or pass the time, whether individually or in groups.

Coffeehouses are thought to have started in the Ottoman Empire, which ruled much of the eastern Mediterranean from its capital of Constantinople present-day Istanbul. Various legends circulate about coffee being served in a public place in Istanbul in the late 1400s, but documentation is lacking. In 1530 the first coffeehouse in Damascus was opened, and not long after there were many coffeehouses in Cairo. The first two coffeehouses known to have existed in Constantinople were both established about 1555.

In the 16th or 17th century, coffee appeared for the first time in western Europe, to be followed by coffeehouses, which quickly became popular. The first, recorded in 1645, was in Venice, due to its trade with the Ottoman Empire.

England saw its first coffeehouse in 1650. The building, in Oxford, still exists as a trendy cocktail bar. The same city's Queen's Lane Coffee House, established in 1654, is also still inexistence today. The first coffeehouse in London was opened in 1652, by Pasqua Rosée, the servant of a trader in Turkish goods named Daniel Edwards, who imported the coffee and assisted Rosée in setting up the establishment. Within 25 years, there were more than 3,000 coffeehouses in England. In 1672 Rosée established the first coffeehouse in Paris, and held a city-wide coffee monopoly until the Café Procope opened 14 years later. The Procope became a major meeting place of the philosophers of the French Enlightenment. America had its first coffeehouse in Boston, in 1676, and Austria's was opened in Vienna in 1685.

The banning of women from coffeehouses was not universal, but does appear to have been common in Europe. In Germany, women frequented them, but in England and France they were banned. In an engraving of a Parisian coffeehouse of around 1700, the gentlemen sit at long communal tables strewn with papers and writing implements. Coffeepots are ranged at an open fire, with a hanging cauldron of boiling water. The only woman present presides, separated in a canopied booth, from which she serves coffee in tall cups.

By the 18th century, coffeehouses were entrenched in London's cultural landscape, becoming meeting places where business could be carried out, news exchanged and government announcements read. By 1739 there were 551 of these establishments in London; each attracted a particular clientele divided by occupation or attitude, such as lawyers, booksellers and authors, or men of fashion.

Jonathan's Coffee House saw the listing of stock and commodity prices for the dealers who formed the majority of its patrons, and this activity later evolved into the Stock Exchange. Meanwhile, the use of salesrooms attached to other coffeehouses provided the start for the great auction houses of Sotheby's and Christie's. The Jerusalem was established by 1735, and its address was given in various Londondirectories for a number of merchants active in import and export.

Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse, established in the late 17th century, was perhaps one of the best known in London. Before long, the majority of its clients were sailors and others using or working in shipping. Lloyd's developed an agreement with the Post Office to pass on news of various ships directly to the customers of the coffeehouse, so that those involved would be the first to know of either disaster or success for their ventures. This eventually became the Lloyd's List, first published in 1734. By the early 19th century, Lloyd's was less of a coffeehouse and more of an insurance business.

While some coffeehouses in the 17th and 18th centuries became the offices and meeting rooms of businessmen, others evolved into centres of debate and teaching, the venue for lectures-particularly on scientific subjects.

Many lecturers put on spectacular shows explaining scientific principles and techniques to a non-specialist audience. They frequently used apparatus they had built themselves, which could then be bought or commissioned from them by members of the audience. A particularly popular demonstration used a planetarium to show the movement of the planets around the sun in our solar system.

Coffeehouses were often called Penny Universities because of the cheap education they provided. For an entrance fee of one penny, visitors could read the newspapers, listen to lecturers and engage in discussion on any number of topics.

Coffeehouses declined during the 19th century as other institutions replaced many of their original functions. Businesses now had their own offices, while a whole range of societies developed, catering for every scientific and intellectual interest.
